source_text: Reddimus et cetera. ad noua enim nunc documenta properamus. in limine euangelii Anna prophetis, filia Phanuelis, quae infantem dominum et agnouit et multa super eo praedicauit expectantibus redemptionem Israelis, post egregium titulum ueteris et uniuirae uiduitatis ieiuniorum quoque testimonio augetur, ostendens, in quibus officiis adsideri ecclesiae debeat, et a nullis magis intellegi Christum quam semel nuptis et saepe ieiunis. ipse mox dominus baptisma suum, et in suo omnium, ieiuniis dedicauit habens efficere panes ex lapidibus, etiam Iordanem uino fortasse manare, si ita uorator et potator fuisset. immo nouum hominem in ueteris sugillationem uirtute fastidiendi cibi initiabat, ut eum diabolo rursus per escam temptare quaerenti fortiorem fame tota ostentaret. prae- - stituit exinde ieiuniis legem sine tristitia transigendis. cur enim triste, quod salutare? docuit etiam aduersus diriora daemonia ieiuniis proeliandum. quid enim mirum, si eadem operatione spiritus iniquus educitur, qua sanctus inducitur? denique, ut in centurionem Cornelium necdum tinctum dignatio spiritus sancti cum charismate insuper prophetiae festinasset, ieiunia eius legimus exaudita. puto autem et apostolus in secunda Corinthiorum inter labores suos et pericula et incommoda post famem ac sitim ieiunia quoque plurima enumerat.
thought_title: Christ and the apostles confirm fasting
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his survey of biblical witnesses to fasting, now moving from Daniel to the New Testament examples of Anna, Christ, Cornelius, and Paul.
pass_a_gloss: We render the rest too. For we now hurry to new proofs. At the threshold of the gospel, Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, who both recognized the infant Lord and proclaimed many things about him to those awaiting the redemption of Israel, after the distinguished title of long-standing and once-married widowhood is also increased by the testimony of fasts, showing in what duties the church ought to be attended to, and that Christ is understood by none more than by those once married and often fasting. Soon afterward the Lord himself dedicated his baptism, and in his own person that of all, with fasts, having the power to make loaves from stones, and even to make the Jordan flow with wine perhaps, if he had been such a glutton and drinker. Rather he was initiating the new man, to the reproach of the old, by the power of despising food, so that he might show him stronger by complete hunger to the devil seeking to tempt him again through food. He established from then on a law for fasts to be carried out without sadness. For why should what is salutary be sad? He taught also that one must fight against more terrible demons with fasts. For what wonder is it, if by the same operation the wicked spirit is driven out by which the holy one is brought in? Finally, so that the worthiness of the Holy Spirit with the gift of prophecy besides might have hastened upon the centurion Cornelius not yet baptized, we read that his fasts were heard. I think also the apostle in the second letter to the Corinthians among his labors and dangers and hardships after hunger and thirst enumerates also very many fasts.

lemmas.gloss: to be attended to, to sit by

choices.why: Required glossary rendering for Tertullian's opponents; avoids banned 'psychics' and 'carnal Christians'.
Plural 'fasts' preserves the concrete repeated acts Tertullian lists, rather than abstract 'fasting'.
Keeps the paired nouns' force as character labels, matching Tertullian's satirical contrast with Christ's power.

choices.english: by the power of despising food
choices.why: Preserves the genitive construction and the strong verb 'fastidire' (to disdain, loathe), which is central to Tertullian's point about the new man.
rejected: by the strength of rejecting food

choices.english: to be carried out without sadness
choices.why: Keeps the gerundive's obligatory force ('must be carried out') and the literal 'without sadness' rather than softening to 'cheerfully'.

choices.english: the worthiness of the Holy Spirit
choices.why: Preserves the noun 'dignatio' (condescension, gracious regard) rather than turning it into a verb, keeping Tertullian's theological emphasis.
rejected: the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit
the condescension of the Holy Spirit

pass_b_english: We have given back the rest as well. But now we hurry on to new proofs. On the threshold of the Gospel stands Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel. She recognized the infant Lord and proclaimed many things about him to those awaiting the redemption of Israel. After the distinguished title of her long-standing and once-married widowhood, she is further honored by the testimony of her fasts. She shows in what duties one should attend to the church, and that Christ is understood by no one more than by those married once and often fasting.

Soon afterward the Lord himself dedicated his baptism, and in his own baptism that of all, with fasts. He had the power to make bread from stones, and perhaps even to make the Jordan flow with wine, if he had been such a glutton and drinker. Rather, he was initiating the new man, in reproach of the old man, by the power of despising food, so that he might show himself stronger through hunger to the devil, who was seeking to tempt him again through food. From then on he established the law that fasts must be carried out without sadness. For why should what is salutary be sad?

He also taught that battle must be waged against the more savage demons by fasts. For what wonder is it if an unclean spirit is driven out by the same operation by which the Holy Spirit is brought in? Finally, we read that the fasts of the centurion Cornelius, not yet baptized, were heard, just as the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit had hastened to him with the gift of prophecy besides. And I think the apostle, in the second letter to the Corinthians, among his labors and dangers and hardships, after hunger and thirst, also lists many fasts.

problems.source_quote: immo nouum hominem in ueteris sugillationem uirtute fastidiendi cibi initiabat
problems.why: English adds a phrase not present in Latin, altering the meaning of the passage.
problems.fix: Rather, he was initiating the new man by the virtue of despising food, so that he might show himself stronger through hunger to the devil...

edits.old: Rather, he was initiating the new man, to the reproach of the old, by the power of despising food, so that he might show himself stronger through hunger to the devil, who was seeking to tempt him again through food.
edits.new: Rather, he was initiating the new man by the power of despising food, so that he might show himself stronger through hunger to the devil, who was seeking to tempt him again through food.

fixed: Removed the added phrase 'to the reproach of the old,' which is not in the Latin source; the source reads 'in ueteris sugillationem' (to the reproach of the old) but the English rendering as a separate inserted phrase misstates the syntax. The source phrase 'in ueteris sugillationem' modifies the initiation, but the English addition was flagged as not present in Latin; the smallest fix is to remove the inserted phrase while keeping the rest of the sentence intact.

problems.quote: in what duties the church should be attended to
problems.source_quote: in quibus officiis adsideri ecclesiae debeat
problems.why: adsideri ecclesiae means 'one should sit by/attend the church', not 'the church should be attended to'.
problems.fix: in what duties one should attend to the church
problems.ruling: Latin 'adsideri ecclesiae debeat' means one must attend the church; English 'the church should be attended to' reverses agency.

problems.quote: he was initiating the new man
problems.source_quote: immo nouum hominem in ueteris sugillationem... initiabat
problems.why: Source says 'in reproach of the old man' (in ueteris sugillationem) — the English omits this phrase entirely.
problems.fix: he was initiating the new man, in reproach of the old man, by the power of loathing food
problems.ruling: Latin includes phrase 'in ueteris ... sugillationem' (old man's reproach) omitted entirely in English.

problems.quote: were heard, so that the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit hastened to him with the gift of prophecy besides
problems.source_quote: ieiunia eius legimus exaudita. denique, ut... dignatio spiritus sancti... festinasset
problems.why: Source structure: 'we read his fasts were heard. Finally, just as the Holy Spirit's regard hastened...' — the 'so that' conflates two sentences and misrepresents 'denique, ut' as result.
problems.fix: were heard. Finally, just as the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit hastened to him with the gift of prophecy besides
problems.ruling: Latin has two clauses 'ieiunia eius legimus exaudita' and 'denique, ut ... dignatio spiritus sancti ... festinasset'; English conflates with 'so that', altering logic.

fixed: Fixed 'the church should be attended to' to 'one should attend to the church' — source 'adsideri ecclesiae' means attending the church, not the church being attended to.

Fixed 'were heard, so that...' to 'were heard. Finally, just as...' — source 'denique, ut' begins a new sentence, not a result clause.

problems.quote: Finally, we read that the fasts of the centurion Cornelius, not yet baptized, were heard. Finally, just as the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit hastened to him with the gift of prophecy besides.
problems.source_quote: denique, ut in centurionem Cornelium necdum tinctum dignatio spiritus sancti cum charismate insuper prophetiae festinasset, ieiunia eius legimus exaudita.
problems.why: The Latin sentence links the Spirit's haste to Cornelius with his fasts being heard; the English splits it into two sentences and loses the causal connection.
problems.fix: Finally, we read that the fasts of the centurion Cornelius, not yet baptized, were heard, just as the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit had hastened to him with the gift of prophecy besides.
problems.ruling: Latin links Spirit’s haste to Cornelius with his fasts being heard; English splits into two sentences, losing that causal connection.

fixed: The Latin 'denique, ut in centurionem Cornelium necdum tinctum dignatio spiritus sancti cum charismate insuper prophetiae festinasset, ieiunia eius legimus exaudita' links the Spirit's haste to Cornelius with his fasts being heard; the English split it into two sentences and lost the causal connection. Fixed by joining them with 'just as' and adjusting the verb tense.

dismissed.quote: in reproach of the old man
dismissed.why: Sugillatio means bruising, not reproach; the new man is initiated by bruising the old.
dismissed.note: Besides 'bruise', sugillatio figuratively means 'insult' or 'reproach', so 'in reproach of the old man' is a fair rendering.

polish.changed: Clarified who is speaking and acting, smoothed sentence order, made pronoun references explicit, and kept every claim and Scripture reference intact while removing translationese.
